# Agentic AI Courses in 2026: An Honest Comparison

> Agentic AI courses split into four types that barely compete. What each one leaves you with, the prerequisite trap, and how to pick in ten minutes.

- [About](/about)

- [Use Cases](/use-cases)

- [Curriculum](/curriculum)

- [For Companies](/corporate)

- [Pricing](/immersive)

- [Blog](/blog)

- [Enroll](/enroll)

[Secure Your Spot](/enroll)

[← Blog](/blog)

AI Skills

## Agentic AI courses in 2026: an honest comparison.

Marliis Schneider

August 20, 2026

7 min read

![Agentic AI courses in 2026: an honest comparison.](../images/blog/agentic-ai-courses-2026-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- “Agentic AI course” now describes four products that barely compete with each other: university certificates, cloud-vendor training paths, marketplace video courses, and in-person build programs.

- The question that separates them is not the syllabus. It is what you have running when you finish. Most produce a certificate. Few produce a deployed agent.

- Microsoft and IBM publish genuinely free agentic AI material. If a paid course only teaches concepts, that free material is your benchmark for whether the price is doing anything.

- Prerequisites are the trap. Several courses labelled for beginners assume you already write Python, and say so only once you are inside.

Search for “agentic AI course” and the first page hands you Johns Hopkins, Carnegie Mellon, MIT, Google, Microsoft, Udemy, Udacity and Coursera in one list. They are priced from zero to five figures. They are not alternatives to each other, and nothing on that page tells you which one matches what you are trying to do.

Here is the sorting logic we use when people ask us this, including the cases where the answer is not us.

### “Agentic AI course” describes four different products

**University certificate programs.** The [Johns Hopkins agentic AI certificate](https://online.lifelonglearning.jhu.edu/jhu-certificate-program-agentic-ai), [Carnegie Mellon’s program](https://execonline.cs.cmu.edu/agentic-ai-program) and [MIT’s Applied Agentic AI for Organizational Transformation](https://professionalprograms.mit.edu/online-program-agentic-ai-organizational-transformation/) sit here. You are buying a credential with a recognisable name on it, delivered online over several weeks, usually built around cases and frameworks rather than shipping software.

**Cloud-vendor training paths.** [Microsoft Learn](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/paths/gh-developing-agentic-systems-1) and [Google Skills](https://www.skills.google/paths/3273) teach agents inside their own stack. These are accurate, current, and free or near-free. They are also, reasonably, about their platform.

**Marketplace video courses.** [Udemy](https://www.udemy.com/course/the-complete-agentic-ai-engineering-course/), [Udacity](https://www.udacity.com/course/agentic-ai--nd900), [Coursera](https://www.coursera.org/courses?query=agentic%20ai), [DeepLearning.AI](https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/agentic-ai). Deep, self-paced, cheap relative to the universities. Completion is the problem, not content.

**In-person build programs.** A cohort in a room for a fixed stretch, building on your own work. Far fewer of these exist because they do not scale. MakerSquare is one; we are in Austin.

### What each type actually leaves you with

| Type | Assumes you code? | What you have at the end | Credential |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| University certificate | Sometimes | Frameworks, case analysis, a plan | Yes, and it carries weight |
| Cloud-vendor path | Usually yes | Working knowledge of one platform | Badge |
| Marketplace video course | Often yes, stated late | Notes, sample repos, unfinished projects | Certificate of completion |
| In-person build program | No | A deployed agent doing your real work | Usually none |

That last column is the honest trade. If you need the credential for a promotion case or a procurement process, the universities win and nothing else is close. If you need something running by month end, a certificate does not help you.

### The prerequisite trap

This is where most non-technical people lose money. A course can be genuinely introductory about *agents* and still assume you are fluent in Python, virtual environments and API keys. The listing says beginner. It means beginner to agents, not beginner to programming.

Before paying, find the actual first exercise. If it opens a terminal or a notebook and starts with `pip install`, you now know what the course really requires. That is not a knock on the course. It is a mismatch you can detect in two minutes.

The related question is worth separating too: [using AI and building with AI are different skills](/blog/using-ai-vs-building-with-ai), and a lot of course titles blur them deliberately.

### What a certificate in agentic AI is worth

Two things, and it is worth being precise about which you are buying.

A university certificate is a signal to other people: a hiring manager, a promotion committee, a client. It travels. It is also the expensive option, and it is generally not evidence that you can build anything.

A completion certificate from a video marketplace is a signal to nobody. That is not cynicism, it is just how they are read. Buy those courses for the content if the content is good, and ignore the certificate.

Neither is the same as a working agent you can open in a meeting. If that is what you actually want, optimise for it directly rather than hoping it falls out of a syllabus.

### How to choose in about ten minutes

Answer three questions in order.

**Do you need a credential with a name on it?** If yes, stop here and pick the university program you can afford. Nothing else substitutes.

**Can you already write code?** If yes, the free Microsoft and Google paths plus a marketplace course will get you a long way for very little, and you should start there before spending real money.

**If no to both** — you cannot code, and you want something running rather than a certificate — then self-paced video is the format that fails you most often, and the thing to look for is a program with a deadline, a room, and a requirement that you ship. That is the category we built MakerSquare for, and if Austin does not work for you, the criterion still holds: find the one that makes you deploy something.

If you want the same comparison across general AI programs rather than agent-specific ones, we keep one at [best AI courses and bootcamps in 2026](/blog/best-ai-courses-bootcamps-2026), and a direct [MakerSquare vs. Wharton, UT Austin and General Assembly breakdown](/comparison).

Frequently asked questions

Which course is best for agentic AI?

There is no single best one, because “agentic AI course” covers four different products. If you need a recognised credential, a university certificate from Johns Hopkins, Carnegie Mellon or MIT is the only category that delivers it. If you already write code, the free Microsoft Learn and Google Skills paths cover the ground cheaply. If you cannot code and want something actually running at the end, look for an in-person program with a deadline and a shipping requirement, because self-paced video is the format that fails that goal most often.

How do I learn agentic AI?

Start by checking whether the material assumes programming. Free official paths from Microsoft and IBM teach the concepts well, so use those as your benchmark before paying for anything. Then build one small agent against your own real work rather than a tutorial dataset — the gap between following a walkthrough and shipping something that runs on your data is where most of the learning actually is.

How can I become certified in agentic AI?

Certification comes from university executive-education programs — Johns Hopkins, Carnegie Mellon and MIT all run agentic AI certificates online over several weeks. Cloud vendors issue badges for their own platforms. Completion certificates from video marketplaces are a different thing and are generally not read as credentials by hiring managers, so buy those courses for the content rather than the certificate.

Where do I learn agentic AI?

Free and official: Microsoft Learn, Google Skills and IBM’s Cognitive Class. Paid and self-paced: DeepLearning.AI, Udemy, Udacity, Coursera. Credentialed: Johns Hopkins, Carnegie Mellon, MIT. In person and build-focused: a small number of cohort programs, including MakerSquare in Austin. Pick the row that matches whether you need a credential, a skill or a shipped product.

# AI Adoption Strategy for Non-Technical Teams: What Works

> What actually works for AI adoption on non-technical teams, which approaches keep failing, and how to build a rollout that survives 30 days.

[← Blog](/blog)

AI Adoption

## AI adoption strategy for non-technical teams: what works.

Marliis Schneider

July 8, 2026

5 min read

![AI adoption strategy for non-technical teams: what works.](../images/blog/ai-adoption-nontechnical-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- Non-technical teams don't need a different kind of AI — they need a different kind of rollout. Access-first strategies consistently underperform structure-first ones.

- The three things that separate successful AI rollouts: specific use cases, more than five hours of applied practice, and peer accountability structures.

- BCG research shows that companies with intentional AI training strategies achieve 67% higher ROI and adopt 2.3x faster — this is especially relevant for non-technical teams where self-directed learning stalls out fastest.

- Starting with a problem your team already cares about — not a feature of the tool — is the fastest path to genuine adoption.

Most AI rollouts for non-technical teams fail at the same point: the initial excitement. There's a kickoff, a demo, maybe a workshop. People are interested. Then they go back to their desks and... mostly don't use it. Not because they're resistant. Because "explore what AI can do for you" is not actually an instruction they can follow.

The right AI adoption strategy for non-technical teams is not about finding a simpler tool or a shorter tutorial. It's about designing the rollout itself differently — with the specificity, structure, and accountability that make behavior change stick. Here's what that looks like.

### What fails: the access-first approach

The most common approach to AI adoption looks like this: procure licenses, announce the rollout, provide some introductory materials, and wait. This is the access-first approach, and it's the approach that produces the "over 80% of companies reporting no measurable productivity gains" finding from G-P's 2026 survey of 6,000 executives.

The assumption behind access-first is that the limiting factor is tool availability. Once people have the tool, they'll figure out how to use it. This assumption is wrong for most non-technical teams. The limiting factor is not access — it's the absence of a clear starting task, a peer group to learn alongside, and enough structured practice time to develop actual judgment with the tool.

BCG's research makes this concrete: among companies that paired AI deployment with intentional training strategies, ROI ran 67% higher and adoption was 2.3x faster than among companies that deployed without that structure. The structure isn't a nice-to-have. It's what drives the result.

### What works: problem-first, then tool

The fastest path to real AI adoption for non-technical teams starts with a problem the team already cares about. Not a feature of the AI tool — a problem in the team's actual work.

This sounds obvious, but it's the opposite of how most rollouts work. Most rollouts lead with the tool: "Here's Claude, here's what it can do, go try it." The effective version leads with the problem: "We currently spend four hours a week on competitive research. We're going to figure out whether AI can cut that to one hour."

When the problem is specific, the rollout becomes specific. You know what success looks like. You know what to practice. You can measure whether it worked. And crucially, team members have a reason to invest the learning time — they're solving something real, not experimenting in the abstract.

McKinsey's 2025 research on workplace AI adoption found that teams that identified specific use cases before general rollout were significantly more likely to report sustained adoption three months later. Problem-first works. Feature-first doesn't.

### Building accountability into the structure

The second element that separates working rollouts from failed ones is accountability. Not surveillance — accountability. Some structure that makes trying things with AI the default, rather than an extra effort on top of regular work.

This can be simple. A weekly five-minute team slot where one person shares what they tried with AI and what happened. A shared document where the team logs their prompts and results. A clear expectation from the manager that a specific task should be done with AI as the default for the next 30 days.

The key insight from BCG's research is the five-hour threshold: employees who cross five or more hours of applied AI practice are dramatically more likely to become regular users (79%) than those who stay below that threshold (67%). The accountability structure is what gets non-technical teams across that threshold. Without it, most people hit a moment of friction, don't immediately see the value, and quietly stop trying.

### What this means for professionals and managers building their own AI capability

If you're trying to build AI capability for yourself or a small team, the same principles apply. The question isn't "what's the best AI tool?" It's "what's the specific task I want to change, and what does done-with-AI look like for that task?"

MakerSquare is a 2-week in-person AI builder program in Austin, TX — we work with operators, founders, and professionals who want to build real AI tools, not just use them. The structure of the program provides exactly what most self-directed AI learning lacks: a specific problem to solve, a peer group going through it together, and daily accountability to actually build things. See what the [curriculum](https://www.makersquare.ai/curriculum) covers, or read about [what the research shows about AI ROI](https://www.makersquare.ai/blog/how-to-get-roi-from-ai-at-work).

Non-technical teams don't need a simpler AI. They need a smarter rollout.

Frequently asked questions

What is the best AI adoption strategy for non-technical teams?

The most effective AI adoption strategy for non-technical teams combines three elements: specific use cases (not general 'explore AI' directives), structured practice time above the five-hour threshold where regular adoption kicks in, and peer accountability built into the rollout. Generic awareness training without these three elements consistently fails to change behavior.

How do you introduce AI to a team that isn't technical?

Start with a problem, not a tool. Identify a specific task the team already finds slow or tedious, then introduce AI as a way to address that specific problem. Non-technical teams adopt AI faster when it's presented as a solution to something they already care about — not as a general capability to explore.

What AI tools work best for non-technical teams?

Claude and ChatGPT are the most versatile for non-technical teams because they require no setup and work through plain-language instructions. For more structured workflows, tools like Notion AI, Zapier with AI integrations, and Google Workspace's AI features sit directly in existing work environments. The best tool is the one that fits into where the team already works — not the most powerful standalone option.

How long does it take for a non-technical team to become proficient with AI?

BCG research establishes five or more hours of structured, applied AI practice as the threshold for regular adoption. For non-technical teams specifically, reaching that threshold through deliberate practice on real work tasks typically takes four to eight weeks of consistent use — not the two or three sessions that most corporate rollouts provide.

# AI Automation for Non-Engineers: What's Actually Possible

> AI automation has moved past chatbots. An honest look at the multi-step workflows and custom tools you can build without writing code.

- [About](/about)

- [Use Cases](/use-cases)

- [Curriculum](/curriculum)

- [For Companies](/corporate)

- [Enroll](/enroll)

[Secure Your Spot](/enroll)

[← Blog](/blog)

Build with AI

## AI automation for non-engineers: what's actually possible

Marliis Schneider

August 18, 2026

5 min read

![AI automation for non-engineers: what](../images/blog/ai-automation-non-engineers-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- AI automation for non-engineers is genuinely mature in 2026 — multi-step workflows, custom AI tools, and intelligent business automations are all within reach without writing code.

- The meaningful distinction is between automating structured data movement (old automation) and automating tasks that involve unstructured inputs and intelligent synthesis (AI automation).

- The realistic ceiling for non-engineer AI automation is higher than most people think — and lower than the hype suggests. Understanding both sides prevents wasted effort.

- The tools — Make, Zapier, Claude, n8n — are designed for non-technical users. The constraint is problem clarity, not technical skill.

There's a lot of noise about what's possible with AI automation and what requires an engineering team. This post is an honest account of both sides — what non-engineers can actually build today, and where you'll still hit a wall without technical help.

**The short answer: AI automation for non-engineers is far more capable than it was 18 months ago, and far less limited than most non-technical professionals assume.** You can build multi-step workflows, custom AI assistants, automated reporting pipelines, and intelligent document generators — all without writing code. Here's what that looks like in practice, and where the real limits are.

### What's genuinely within reach for non-engineers

The category of AI automation that's solidly accessible to non-engineers is any workflow where: (1) the inputs are available in digital form, (2) the processing task is synthesis, writing, or classification, and (3) the output follows a defined format.

Concretely, this includes: automated meeting summaries and action item extraction from call recordings, document generation from structured inputs (proposals, SOPs, client reports), custom AI assistants trained on company knowledge that can answer questions and route inquiries, competitive intelligence briefs assembled from multiple sources, and internal workflow automations that route information based on AI classification (e.g., an email triage system that categorizes and prioritizes incoming messages).

These are not toy examples. These are tools that meaningfully change how people work, and they can be built by a non-engineer with a few weeks of focused learning. According to [Zapier's 2025 automation research](https://zapier.com/blog/state-of-automation/), the average non-technical user who builds their first multi-step automation reclaims 5 hours per week within 30 days of deployment. The learning curve is real; the payoff is real too.

### What still requires engineering help

Being honest about the limits is important. AI automation for non-engineers has a ceiling, and hitting it without knowing it's there is frustrating.

You'll need engineering help when: you need to process data at high volume and low latency (thousands of records per hour), you need custom integrations with systems that don't have native Make or Zapier connectors, you need to build user-facing products with login, permissions, and database architecture, or when error handling and reliability need to be production-grade. These aren't insurmountable — they're engineering problems, and they're worth knowing about before you start a build.

The good news is that most internal business automation — the kind that saves your team 10 hours a week — doesn't require any of this. The problems that need engineers are usually customer-facing products or high-scale data pipelines. The problems that need operators and professionals are the ones that AI automation for non-engineers is built for.

### The tools that make this possible in 2026

Three categories of tools have made AI automation genuinely accessible to non-engineers:

**AI intelligence tools:** Claude and ChatGPT (and their Projects/Custom GPT features) allow you to create persistent, configured AI assistants that have context about your business. These can be connected to other tools via API without writing code — both platforms expose this through Make and Zapier integrations.

**Automation platforms:** Make, Zapier, and n8n are the main options. Make is the most powerful for complex workflows. Zapier is the easiest for simple ones. n8n is open-source and self-hostable for teams that want more control without a developer. All three have visual interfaces and extensive libraries of pre-built connectors.

**Data and storage:** Airtable and Notion serve as the data layer for most no-code AI workflows. They connect easily to Make and Zapier, have AI features built in, and can serve as both the input source and output destination for automated processes.

According to [McKinsey's 2025 AI adoption research](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai), organizations where non-technical staff have built their own AI tools see faster adoption and higher ROI than those where AI is implemented top-down by IT. The pattern is consistent: proximity to the problem produces better tools.

### What this means for non-engineers ready to build

The threshold question isn't "am I technical enough?" It's "do I know the problem well enough to design a solution?" Non-engineers who understand their business problems deeply are often better positioned to build effective AI automations than engineers who understand the tools but not the work.

MakerSquare is a 2-week in-person AI builder program in Austin, TX — built for operators, founders, and professionals who want to build real AI tools, not just use them. The curriculum is designed to take non-engineers from concept to working automation in 14 days. See exactly what that covers at [makersquare.ai/curriculum](https://www.makersquare.ai/curriculum).

Frequently asked questions

What can non-engineers automate with AI?

Non-engineers can automate a significant range of business tasks with AI: document generation (proposals, reports, SOPs), research synthesis and competitive briefs, email drafting and follow-up sequences, data entry and CRM updates, meeting summaries and action item extraction, and customer-facing chatbots trained on company knowledge. The tools required — Make, Zapier, Claude Projects, Airtable — are all designed for non-technical users.

Do I need to code to use AI automation tools?

No. Tools like Make, Zapier, and n8n have visual, drag-and-drop interfaces that allow non-technical users to build multi-step automations. The AI layer (Claude, ChatGPT) is configured through natural language instructions. You do not need to write code to build a workflow that takes data from one tool, sends it to an AI for processing, and routes the output to another tool.

What is the most useful first AI automation for a small business?

The most useful first automation depends on your business, but the highest-ROI starting points are usually: a weekly report or status update generator, a customer inquiry response drafting tool, or a document generator for proposals or quotes. These are high-frequency, high-time-cost tasks that follow predictable structures — exactly what AI handles best, and exactly what you can automate without code.

What's the difference between AI automation and regular automation?

Traditional automation (like Zapier's basic workflows) moves data from one place to another in a fixed pattern. AI automation adds intelligence — the ability to interpret, synthesize, write, and make judgment calls within defined parameters. This means AI automation can handle unstructured inputs (an email, a voice memo, a meeting transcript) and produce structured, usable outputs, rather than just routing structured data between systems.

# AI Bootcamp vs. Online Course: Which One Works | MakerSquare

> Most professionals who start an online AI course never finish. Research on completion rates, outcomes, and what in-person training delivers differently.

[← Blog](/blog)

AI at Work

## In-person AI program vs. online course: which actually changes your career?

Marliis Schneider

June 25, 2026

5 min read

![In-person AI program vs. online course: which actually changes your career?](../images/blog/ai-bootcamp-vs-course-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- Research consistently finds that fewer than 15% of people who start a self-paced online course finish it. For AI courses specifically, completion rates are often closer to 3 to 6 percent.

- BCG found that professionals who receive five or more hours of structured AI training are 79% more likely to become regular AI users, compared to those who haven't crossed that threshold.

- The gap between formats is not content. It's structure: accountability, compressed time, real projects, and learning with people working on the same problems.

- Online courses make sense for exploring a topic. In-person intensives make sense when the goal is to actually change how you work.

Online AI courses have a completion rate between 3 and 6 percent. That's not a criticism — it's a structural fact about what the format is optimized for. The question worth asking isn't whether online learning is good or bad. It's whether it can deliver what you're actually trying to accomplish. If the goal is exposure to AI concepts, a self-paced course is a reasonable starting point. If the goal is to change how you work, the completion data makes a strong case for a different format.

This isn't a knock on online learning as a category. It's a structural argument: what online courses are optimized for and what in-person intensives are optimized for are not the same thing. Understanding the difference makes it easier to choose the right one for the right goal.

At our Demo Night last week, one of the people who enrolled told us she'd already taken two online AI courses — good ones, well-reviewed, from credible platforms. She understood how AI worked. She just couldn't point to anything that had changed about how she actually did her job. That gap is the structural problem this post is about.

### What online AI courses actually deliver

The online AI course market is enormous. Coursera, Udemy, DeepLearning.AI, fast.ai, and dozens of newer platforms offer courses ranging from free to a few hundred dollars, covering everything from prompt engineering to building AI agents. The content quality, in many cases, is genuinely good. Instructors with real depth, well-structured modules, practical exercises.

What online courses deliver well: structured exposure to a topic, the ability to learn at your own pace, breadth of coverage across AI tools and concepts, and low financial risk. For someone who wants to understand what large language models are, how vector databases work, or what the current tooling landscape looks like, an online course is a reasonable place to start.

What they do not deliver well is accountability, application, and the compression of learning that comes from having to ship something by a deadline in front of other people. That gap is where most learners stall.

### The completion problem

The completion rate data on online courses is consistent enough to be treated as a structural fact of the format. Researchers at MIT and Harvard who studied massive open online courses found completion rates of 3 to 6 percent across tens of millions of enrollments. Paid platforms with more friction to enter perform better, but industry data still shows that fewer than 15% of learners who enroll in a self-paced online course complete it.

#### Why motivated people still quit

This isn't primarily a motivation problem. Most people who start an online AI course are motivated enough to enroll, pay, and begin. What erodes is the structure: no deadline, no one waiting for your work, no cost to stopping and restarting or never returning. The course stays in the library. Life continues. The skills don't compound because the practice doesn't happen consistently enough.

The implication for AI specifically is significant. Learning to work with AI tools is more like learning to cook than learning a fact. Understanding how a large language model works doesn't change how you work. Using one on your actual job tasks, failing, iterating, and building judgment about when it's useful and when it isn't: that's what changes how you work. Self-paced online formats make that harder to sustain.

### What in-person AI training delivers differently

The difference an in-person intensive delivers is not curriculum. Most of the content covered in a well-designed in-person AI program is available somewhere online. The difference is what the structure forces you to do.

In-person programs impose external deadlines. You're not learning toward a vague goal of "getting better at AI." You have a project due at the end of the week, and the person next to you is watching you figure it out. That pressure changes how learning happens. The moments where you're stuck, confused, or tempted to move on without understanding become the moments where instructors intervene and peers fill the gap. That's the inflection point that most self-directed learners never reach, because there's no one in a YouTube video watching whether you understood section three before moving on to section four.

BCG's AI at Work research identified a threshold at five or more hours of structured training, after which 79% of professionals become consistent AI users. The key word is structured. Structured means someone has designed the sequence, the accountability, the feedback loop, and the outcome you're working toward. Self-paced courses can be well-structured in terms of content. What they can't replicate is a room of people held to the same timeline with the same goal.

For the organizational context, the post on [how to get ROI from AI at work](https://www.makersquare.ai/blog/how-to-get-roi-from-ai-at-work?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=organic_content&utm_campaign=Blog_B2B_ORG_AI-Bootcamp_ATX_EN_Leads&utm_content=MS_ai-bootcamp-vs-online-course_internal-link-01_2026-06-25) covers this from the employer side: the BCG data shows that companies where employees have structured AI training achieve 67% higher ROI than peers without it. That ROI gap comes from skill transfer, not content coverage.

### The cohort effect: why the room matters

There's a second structural advantage to in-person learning that rarely gets mentioned in comparisons: who you're in the room with.

A cohort of professionals working on AI in parallel is not just a social benefit. It's a learning mechanism. When someone in the room figures out a better way to prompt Claude for a financial model, or solves a Cursor problem you've been stuck on for an hour, that knowledge transfers immediately. When you see what someone with a completely different job function builds in two weeks, it expands what you think is possible with the same tools you have access to.

It also changes how you leave. A professional who completes an in-person AI intensive has a network of people who went through the same thing, can debug the same tools, and are experimenting with AI in their own organizations. That network is a continued learning resource in a way that a discussion forum under a Coursera module is not.

For more on what the gap between knowing about AI and being able to use it actually costs, the second post in this series covers [what another year without AI skills actually costs](https://www.makersquare.ai/blog/what-another-year-without-ai-skills-actually-costs?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=organic_content&utm_campaign=Blog_B2B_ORG_AI-Bootcamp_ATX_EN_Leads&utm_content=MS_ai-bootcamp-vs-online-course_internal-link-02_2026-06-25) in concrete career terms.

### Which format is right for you

Online courses make sense if you want to explore whether AI is relevant to your work before committing time or money, if you're looking to understand a specific tool or concept and already have the self-direction to follow through, or if the cost of an in-person program isn't feasible right now.

An in-person intensive makes sense if you've already tried online courses and stalled, if the goal is to build something real and change how your team uses AI, if you're a founder or operator who needs to move quickly and can't afford a six-month learning curve, or if you know that left to your own schedule, this will stay on the list.

The most common version of this we see: someone with a half-completed Coursera certificate and nothing that changed about how they actually work. That's a reasonable starting point. It's also a pretty clear signal.

Frequently asked questions

Is an AI bootcamp worth it compared to online courses?

For most professionals, yes. Online AI courses have completion rates under 15%, and most learners who finish still struggle to apply skills to real work. In-person programs with structured practice and peer accountability produce consistently higher skill transfer and completion rates.

What is the completion rate for online AI courses?

Research on massive open online courses consistently shows completion rates under 15%, with many studies finding averages closer to 3 to 6 percent. Paid platforms with cohort features perform better, but most learners who enroll in a self-paced AI course do not finish it.

How long does it take to learn AI skills in person?

BCG research found that five or more hours of structured AI practice is the threshold at which 79% of professionals become regular AI users. A two-week in-person intensive delivers well above that threshold, with the advantage of compressed time, real projects, and immediate feedback.

What is the difference between an AI bootcamp and an online AI course?

Online courses are self-paced and asynchronous, with no built-in accountability and high dropout rates. In-person AI intensives are cohort-based, scheduled, and project-driven. The key difference is not content but structure: who you build with, whether you ship something real, and whether you are held to a timeline.

# AI for Accountants: What's Changing in 2026 | MakerSquare

> AI is automating accounting busywork — reconciliation, categorization, close — and freeing CPAs for advisory work. What is real and what to do.

- [About](/about)

- [Use Cases](/use-cases)

- [Curriculum](/curriculum)

- [For Companies](/corporate)

- [Pricing](/immersive)

- [Enroll](/enroll)

[Secure Your Spot](/enroll)

[← Blog](/blog)

AI at Work

## AI for Accountants: What's Changing in 2026

Marliis Schneider

August 20, 2026

6 min read

![AI for Accountants: What](../images/blog/ai-for-accountants-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- 46% of accountants now use AI tools daily - up from 18% in 2023 - and 73% of accounting firms have implemented some form of automation, a 340% jump since 2022.

- The Thomson Reuters Institute estimates AI saves an individual CPA about 240 hours a year - roughly $19,000 in recovered capacity at median billing rates.

- The value isn't replacing accountants - it's shifting their time from data entry toward analysis and advisory. AI has already cut the average monthly close by 7.5 days.

- With the profession down more than a third of its licensed workforce since 2019, AI is becoming the practical answer to a real talent shortage - not a threat to the people still in it.

For accountants, the AI conversation in 2026 has moved past 'will it replace us?' to something more useful: which parts of the job it takes off your plate, and what you do with the hours it gives back. The direct answer - AI is automating the repetitive, rules-based work (reconciliation, categorization, first-draft reporting) and pushing accountants toward the analysis and advisory work that actually needs professional judgment. The firms and individuals treating that shift as an opportunity are pulling ahead of the ones treating it as a threat.

### Adoption stopped being early and became normal

The numbers moved fast. 46% of accountants now use AI tools daily, up from just 18% in 2023, and 73% of accounting and CPA firms have implemented some form of automation - a 340% increase from 2022 levels. This isn't a pilot phase anymore. Using AI in accounting work has become a baseline expectation, and the accountants who haven't started are increasingly the exception, not the norm.

Crucially, the people using it are happy with it: 89% of accounting professionals using AI report a positive return on investment. That's an unusually high satisfaction rate for a workplace technology, and it tells you the value is real rather than hype.

### Where the hours actually go back

The most-cited number is striking: the Thomson Reuters Institute estimates AI saves an individual CPA roughly 240 hours per year - about $19,000 in recovered capacity at median billing rates. Across the U.S. profession, that adds up to a projected $12 billion in annual productivity recovery.

Where does the time come from? The repetitive core of the job: transaction categorization, bank reconciliation, accounts payable coding, and first drafts of financial reports. One concrete example - AI adoption has cut the average monthly financial close by 7.5 days. That's a week and a half, every month, moved off the calendar.

### The real shift: from preparer to advisor

Here's the part that matters for your career, not just your calendar. AI adoption has shifted about 8.5% of accountants' time away from routine tasks toward higher-value analysis and advisory work. That's the direction the whole profession is moving: the commodity work (data entry, reconciliation, standard reports) is being automated, and the premium work (interpreting the numbers, advising on decisions, catching what the automation missed) is becoming the job.

This is also why AI reads as help rather than threat to most accountants using it. The profession has lost more than a third of its licensed workforce since 2019. AI isn't arriving into a field with too many people - it's arriving into one with a genuine talent shortage, where automating the routine work is the practical way remaining professionals keep up with demand.

### What this means if you're an accountant building AI skills

The accountants who benefit most aren't the most technical - they're the ones who understand their clients and their books well enough to know exactly what's worth automating and where judgment still has to stay human. That's a skill you can build directly. MakerSquare's [use cases](/use-cases) include building reporting and monitoring tools that pull from real financial data, so the automation fits how you actually work instead of forcing you into a generic tool.

The accountants who thrive in this shift won't be the ones who resisted the automation. They'll be the ones who used the hours it freed to become the advisor their clients can't get from software.

Frequently asked questions

Will AI replace accountants?

No - it's replacing tasks, not accountants. AI automates the repetitive, rules-based work (reconciliation, categorization, first-draft reports) and shifts accountants toward analysis and advisory work that requires judgment. With the profession down over a third of its licensed workforce since 2019, AI is largely filling a talent gap, not eliminating roles.

What accounting tasks can AI automate in 2026?

The reliable ones are transaction categorization, bank reconciliation, accounts payable coding, expense processing, and first drafts of financial reports. More advanced platforms assist with fraud/risk detection and cash-flow forecasting. Judgment-heavy work - tax strategy, audit review, advisory - stays human-led.

How much time does AI actually save accountants?

The Thomson Reuters Institute estimates about 240 hours per CPA per year - roughly $19,000 in recovered capacity at median billing rates. A concrete example: AI adoption has cut the average monthly financial close by about 7.5 days.

Do accountants need to learn to code to use AI?

No. The accountants getting the most value understand their books and clients well enough to know what's worth automating - the tools are directed in plain language, not code. Domain knowledge matters more than technical skill.

Is AI-assisted accounting accurate enough to trust?

AI is reliable for rule-based work (categorization, reconciliation against known rules) but still needs professional review for judgment calls and anomalies. The winning pattern is AI for the repetitive layer plus a human review pass - which is exactly where accountants' expertise now adds the most value.

# AI for Accounting and Bookkeeping: A Non-Accountant's Guide

> AI for accounting is automating bookkeeping, reconciliation, and reporting. Here

[← Blog](/blog)

AI for Business

## AI for accounting and bookkeeping: what non-accountants need to know

Marliis Schneider

August 9, 2026

5 min read

![AI for accounting and bookkeeping: what non-accountants need to know](../images/blog/ai-accounting-bookkeeping-og.webp)

If you run a business and your accounting feels like a quarterly ordeal rather than a real-time view of your finances, AI for accounting is worth understanding. The technology isn't new — QuickBooks has been automating categorization for years — but the sophistication has increased significantly, and the tools accessible to small and mid-size businesses without dedicated finance teams have caught up with what enterprise software has offered for a decade.

This isn't a guide for accountants. It's a guide for business owners, operators, and founders who want to understand what AI is actually automating in finance and what still requires human attention.

Key takeaways

- AI handles transaction categorization, reconciliation, and AP processing reliably — these are now largely automated in leading platforms.

- Financial reporting generation (cash flow summaries, P&L narratives, variance analysis) is where AI delivers significant time savings for leadership teams.

- AI can surface anomalies and flag risks — but it doesn't replace judgment on what to do about them.

- The biggest risk is over-trusting AI categorizations without monthly human review.

- For most small businesses: QuickBooks AI features or Xero with automations enabled are sufficient starting points.

### What AI for accounting actually means

AI for accounting isn't one thing — it's AI applied to specific tasks within the accounting workflow. The clearest way to understand it is by task category:

**Transaction categorization:** AI reads transaction descriptions, amounts, and vendor names, then assigns them to the correct account. QuickBooks, Xero, and FreshBooks have done this for years. The accuracy is high for recurring transactions with familiar vendors; it degrades for ambiguous or novel transactions. Most platforms learn from your corrections over time.

**Bank reconciliation:** AI matches transactions in your accounting system to transactions in your bank feeds, flagging discrepancies for human review. What used to take hours monthly is now largely automated — the human reviews exceptions, not the full match list.

**Accounts payable processing:** AI extracts key data from vendor invoices (vendor name, amount, due date, line items), codes them to the appropriate accounts, and queues them for approval. Tools like Stampli and BILL integrate AI invoice capture that reduces AP data entry by 70–80% for most businesses.

**Expense reporting:** AI reads receipts (via mobile capture), categorizes expenses, matches them to expense policies, and flags policy violations. Expensify and Concur have had this for years; it's now table stakes for any expense management platform.

**Financial reporting:** AI generates narrative summaries of financial statements, highlights variances from prior periods, and answers natural-language questions about financial data. This is the newer, higher-value application — described in detail below.

### The highest-value application for non-accountants: financial reporting narratives

The most significant AI advance for non-accountants in 2026 isn't better categorization — it's the ability to get plain-English explanations of financial data without waiting for your accountant to summarize it for you.

Modern accounting platforms with AI layers (QuickBooks AI, Xero Analytics Plus, and standalone tools like Digits) can generate natural-language explanations of your P&L, flag unusual variances, and answer questions like "why did our gross margin drop this quarter?" by pointing to specific transactions or categories.

For business owners who spend most of their time in operations, not finance, this changes the frequency with which they can engage meaningfully with their numbers. Instead of a monthly accountant call where someone explains what happened, you can ask the system directly — and get a useful answer in seconds.

A McKinsey study on AI in finance found that AI-generated financial narrative tools reduced the time finance teams spend preparing management reports by 40–60%. For small businesses where the owner is the finance team, the impact is even more significant.

### AI for accounts payable: where the ROI is most immediate

If you process more than 50 vendor invoices per month, accounts payable automation is the most immediate ROI opportunity in accounting AI. The workflow is straightforward:

1. Vendor sends invoice to a dedicated email address or portal

2. AI extracts key fields (vendor, amount, due date, line items, purchase order reference)

3. AI suggests GL coding based on vendor history and line item descriptions

4. Human approver reviews and approves (or corrects and approves)

5. Payment is scheduled according to terms

The human involvement is at approval — not at data entry, coding, or scheduling. For businesses processing 200+ invoices per month, this saves 15–20 hours of staff time per month. For smaller businesses, the saving is proportionally smaller, but the accuracy improvement (AI makes fewer data entry errors than humans doing repetitive work) is still meaningful.

BILL (formerly Bill.com) and Stampli are the most widely used small-business AP platforms with strong AI layers. Both integrate with QuickBooks and Xero. Tipalti is the enterprise option for higher-volume, multi-currency operations.

### Cash flow forecasting: where AI helps but doesn't replace judgment

Cash flow forecasting is where AI in accounting is genuinely useful but frequently oversold. AI can analyze historical cash flow patterns, identify seasonal trends, and project forward based on known receivables and payables. It can't know about the large contract you're expecting to close, the equipment purchase you're planning, or the customer who's likely to pay late despite being marked as current.

The practical value: AI forecasting tools (Float, Fathom, and QuickBooks Cash Flow Planner) give you a better baseline to work from and surface patterns in your historical data you might not have noticed. The judgment layer — adjusting for known future events, interpreting the forecast in context, making the actual decisions — remains human.

For businesses with tight cash flow margins, the combination of AI baseline + human adjustments is meaningfully more accurate than either approach alone. Treating AI cash flow forecasts as definitive without human overlay is where businesses get into trouble.

### What AI in accounting still can't do

Understanding the limits is as important as understanding the capabilities:

- **Tax strategy:** AI can organize your data for tax preparation and surface potential deductions based on patterns. It cannot provide tax advice, optimize your structure, or apply judgment to complex multi-state or international situations. A tax professional remains essential for anything beyond simple returns.

- **Audit-grade accuracy:** AI-categorized books require human review before any audit or significant financial transaction. Categorization errors compound. A monthly or quarterly review by someone who understands your business is not optional if you're relying heavily on AI automation.

- **Business context:** AI doesn't know your business strategy. It can't tell you that the $50,000 you spent on a vendor this quarter represents a critical strategic bet that should be interpreted differently from normal expenses. The numbers need human context to become decisions.

- **Anomaly investigation:** AI can flag an anomaly. It can't investigate whether the anomaly represents fraud, a categorization error, an unexpected business development, or a data entry problem. That investigation is human.

### Where to start if you're a small business owner

The right starting point depends on what's currently broken in your accounting workflow:

**If your books are frequently behind:** The issue is usually AP data entry and categorization. Enable AI transaction categorization in QuickBooks or Xero if you haven't, and consider BILL for AP if you're processing meaningful invoice volume. The goal is to get to real-time books, not month-old books.

**If your books are current but you don't understand them:** The issue is reporting. QuickBooks AI reports or a tool like Digits can generate plain-English summaries that make your financial data accessible without an accounting background. Understanding your numbers weekly rather than monthly changes how you run the business.

**If you're spending significant time on expense reports:** Implement Expensify or a similar AI expense tool. The ROI is typically immediate for any business with more than 3–4 people submitting expenses.

MakerSquare is a 2-week in-person AI builder program in Austin, TX — built for operators, founders, and professionals who want to build real AI tools, not just use them. Business owners who attend often build custom reporting dashboards and financial monitoring tools that pull from their existing accounting platforms — giving them real-time financial visibility without waiting on a monthly close.

Frequently asked questions

What accounting tasks can AI automate?

AI currently automates or significantly accelerates: transaction categorization, bank reconciliation, accounts payable processing (invoice capture and coding), expense report processing, and financial report generation. More advanced platforms also automate payroll, tax preparation prep, and cash flow forecasting. The tasks requiring human judgment — tax strategy, audit review, complex structuring — remain human-led.

Can AI replace my bookkeeper?

For simple, consistent bookkeeping, AI tools have largely replaced the work a bookkeeper performed 10 years ago. QuickBooks AI and similar tools categorize transactions, reconcile accounts, and generate reports automatically. However, a good bookkeeper now does more than data entry — they catch categorization errors, flag anomalies, advise on reporting structure, and manage the exceptions AI can't handle. The role has changed more than it has been eliminated.

Is AI-generated financial data reliable?

AI is reliable for rule-based tasks (transaction categorization, reconciliation against known rules) but requires review for judgment calls (ambiguous vendor categorization, multi-period allocation, intercompany transactions). The risk is treating AI-generated categorizations as final without review. A monthly human review of AI-assisted books — looking for categorization errors, misclassified transactions, and anomalies — remains important even with highly automated accounting.

What AI accounting tools are best for small businesses?

For most small businesses: QuickBooks with AI features enabled, or Xero with its automation and app integrations. For businesses with complex AP, Stampli or BILL (formerly Bill.com) AI layers are worth the additional cost. For very small businesses or freelancers, Wave (free) or FreshBooks with AI-assisted categorization is sufficient.

# AI for Business Owners: Where to Start If Non-Technical

> AI for business owners takes no technical skill. Where to start, what to automate first, and which tools actually matter for a small business.

[← Blog](/blog)

AI for Business

## AI for business owners: where to start if you're not technical

Marliis Schneider

August 3, 2026

5 min read

![AI for business owners: where to start if you](../images/blog/ai-for-business-owners-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- AI for business owners doesn't require technical skills — the highest-value applications (customer communication, content, proposals, SOPs) are all accessible with no-code tools.

- Start narrow: one high-frequency task, one tool, one week of practice before adding anything else.

- Small businesses are seeing some of the biggest percentage gains from AI because they're applying it to the tasks the owner was personally doing — which means the leverage goes directly to margin.

- The right frame isn't "replacing staff" — it's "what was taking 3 hours that could take 20 minutes?" That's where AI creates business owner leverage.

Most business owners I talk to have the same hesitation about AI: "I'm not technical enough for this." It's the wrong concern. The AI tools creating the most value for business owners right now don't require any technical skill — they require clarity about what you need and the willingness to iterate on it. Non-technical business owners are seeing some of the biggest gains from AI, because they're applying it to the tasks they were personally doing before.

The right starting point for AI for business owners is simple: find the task that takes you the most time relative to the value it produces, and try AI on that task first. Not an overview of all possible AI applications — one task, one tool, this week.

### The tasks where AI creates the most leverage for business owners

Not every business task is a good fit for AI. The best candidates share three characteristics: they're high-frequency (you do them regularly), they follow a pattern (there's a recognizable structure), and they're currently eating significant time relative to their judgment requirement.

**Customer communication.** Responding to inquiries, writing follow-up emails, handling common questions. A business owner who spends 2 hours a day on email can often cut that to 30–45 minutes with AI drafting the initial responses. The key is building a template that captures your voice and the context about your business — then using AI to fill it in and you to review and send.

**Content and marketing copy.** Social posts, email newsletters, product descriptions, website copy. AI isn't going to replace your brand voice — but it can produce a solid first draft in two minutes that you edit rather than writing from scratch. For a small business owner who knows they should be creating content but never has time, this is often where AI changes the most.

**Proposals and documents.** Client proposals, SOPs, job descriptions, vendor contracts. These follow patterns. Once you've built a template prompt that captures how your proposals are structured, generating a first draft for a new client takes minutes instead of hours.

**Research and competitive analysis.** Understanding a new market, evaluating a vendor, synthesizing industry information. AI tools dramatically compress research tasks — not because they replace primary research, but because they help you synthesize existing information faster.

A 2025 [U.S. Chamber of Commerce survey](https://www.uschamber.com/small-business/state-of-small-business-now) found that 77% of small business owners using AI reported it helped them compete more effectively with larger companies. The mechanisms were consistent: reduced time on administrative tasks, faster content production, and better customer communication.

### The tools that actually matter for small businesses

The AI tool landscape is overwhelming if you approach it as "I need to evaluate everything." You don't. For a non-technical business owner, three tools cover 90% of use cases.

**Claude Pro ($20/month).** Best for: long documents, nuanced writing, analysis of complex situations, anything where you need the AI to follow detailed instructions. Claude's ability to hold a long, complex context makes it the strongest general-purpose tool for business writing and analysis.

**Zapier or Make ($20–$30/month).** Best for: automating repeating workflows that connect multiple apps. When a new lead fills out a form, automatically send a personalized follow-up and add them to your CRM. When a customer places an order, trigger a confirmation and internal notification. No code required — you set up the logic through a visual interface.

**A scheduling or customer-specific AI add-on.** Many vertical-specific tools now have AI built in — email marketing platforms, CRM tools, scheduling software. If you're already paying for Mailchimp, HubSpot, or similar, check whether they've added AI features. Often the best starting point is the AI already inside the tools you use.

According to [Salesforce's 2025 Small Business Trends report](https://www.salesforce.com/resources/research-reports/small-business-trends/), 68% of small businesses using AI tools said they saw positive ROI within the first three months. The fastest ROI came from applications to sales and customer communication.

### The non-obvious insight: owner time is your most expensive resource

Here's something the generic AI-for-business content rarely says directly: for most small business owners, your time is the most expensive resource in the business. If you're billing $200/hour or more on your own work, or if you're doing work that depends entirely on you to function, every hour AI saves you is worth significantly more than an employee hour saved.

This means the calculation for AI investment is different for business owners than for enterprise teams. An enterprise AI tool that saves an analyst 3 hours a week saves the company one analyst-hour of cost. An AI tool that saves a business owner 3 hours a week frees up 3 hours that can go into revenue-generating work — or into not working late on a Tuesday.

The frame that helps: what are you currently doing that a very capable junior person could do if you gave them clear instructions? Those are your AI tasks. Write down your instructions clearly enough that they'd make sense in writing, and that's your prompt.

### What this means for business owners ready to go deeper

Starting with AI is easy. Getting AI to actually change how your business operates takes structure — knowing which tools to use for which tasks, how to build workflows that don't require you to babysit them, and how to iterate toward something that runs without you.

MakerSquare is a 2-week in-person AI builder program in Austin, TX — built for operators, founders, and professionals who want to build real AI tools, not just use them. Business owners who come through the program leave with a working AI system built around their actual business — not a demo, not a tutorial, something they use starting day one back at work. See the [curriculum](https://www.makersquare.ai/curriculum) for what that looks like.

The business owners who are going to look back on this period and say "that's when everything changed" are the ones who started building something real right now — not the ones who waited until it felt less technical.

Frequently asked questions

How can a non-technical business owner start using AI?

Start with one high-frequency, time-consuming task that currently requires you or a team member to do manually. Common first applications: customer communications (drafting email responses, follow-ups), content creation (social posts, blog drafts, product descriptions), and internal document production (reports, proposals, SOPs). Pick one, use Claude or ChatGPT on it for a week, and measure the time saved before adding a second application.

What AI tools are best for small business owners?

For most small business owners, three tools cover the majority of use cases: Claude or ChatGPT (for writing, analysis, and communication), Zapier or Make (for automating repeating workflows without code), and a customer-facing AI tool specific to your industry (if one exists). Start with Claude Pro at $20/month — it's the highest-leverage starting point for most business applications.

What should I automate first in my business with AI?

Automate the tasks that are high-frequency, low-judgment, and currently eating your time or your team's time. The best candidates are: responding to common customer questions, generating first drafts of recurring documents (proposals, reports, status updates), social media content from existing material, and data entry between systems. The goal is to automate the work that takes time but doesn't require your unique judgment.

How much does it cost for a small business to use AI tools?

The core AI tools for small businesses are surprisingly affordable. Claude Pro is $20/month. ChatGPT Plus is $20/month. Zapier's starter plan starts at $20/month. For most small businesses, getting started with AI tools costs $40–60/month — less than a few hours of contractor time. The ROI typically shows up within the first month if you're using the tools on the right tasks.

# AI for Content Creators: Beyond Writing the First Draft

> How to use AI for research, repurposing, SEO, and strategy — not just drafting — so you spend more time on the creative work that matters.

[← Blog](/blog)

AI at Work

## AI for content creators: beyond writing the first draft

Marliis Schneider

July 31, 2026

5 min read

![AI for content creators: beyond writing the first draft](../images/blog/ai-for-content-creators-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- Most content creators use AI for drafting — but the highest-ROI use cases are research, repurposing, and SEO optimization, which are often more time-consuming than writing itself.

- AI for content creators works best as a force multiplier on existing content: one long-form piece becomes a week of multi-platform content with AI-assisted repurposing.

- The creators under competitive pressure from AI are those producing volume of average content; the ones thriving are those whose value is voice, authority, and perspective.

- A 2025 HubSpot survey found content teams using AI produce 3x more content per person — but the quality gap between AI-assisted human content and pure AI content is still significant.

Most content creators who've experimented with AI started the same way: they asked it to write a blog post draft, were mildly impressed, and moved on. The draft was okay. Not their voice. Useful as a starting point. That's where most creators stop — and it's also where the most interesting AI uses for content haven't begun.

The highest-ROI AI applications for content creators in 2026 are not drafting. They're research acceleration, content repurposing, SEO optimization, and strategy work — all things that used to consume hours and can now be compressed dramatically. Here's how it actually plays out in practice.

### Research: compressing the most time-consuming part of content creation

For most content creators, research is the part of content creation that takes the longest and shows up the least in the final product. Finding the right data points, reading the source studies, identifying the counterarguments, synthesizing what other creators have covered — this is genuinely difficult work that AI accelerates without replacing.

The workflow: describe your topic and thesis to Claude, ask what the strongest evidence for and against it is, ask what's been covered extensively by other creators (so you know what to differentiate from), and ask for three specific data points worth including. Then verify the claims and find the primary sources yourself. What used to take two hours of research now takes 30 minutes — the AI sets the map, you verify and fill in the detail.

A 2025 Reuters Institute report on AI in media found that journalists and content producers using AI research assistants reduced pre-writing research time by 45% while maintaining source quality — the key was using AI to identify what to look for, not as a substitute for reading primary sources. 1

### Repurposing: the highest-leverage content workflow

Here's the use case that changes the economics of content creation most fundamentally: AI-assisted repurposing. Take a 2,000-word blog post, a 45-minute podcast episode, or a 20-minute YouTube video. That single piece of content contains enough material for a LinkedIn post, three Twitter threads, a newsletter section, five short-form video hooks, and a Quora answer. Before AI, extracting all of that was a 3–4 hour additional effort. With AI, it's 30 minutes.

The repurposing workflow: paste the transcript or article into Claude, ask it to extract the three most shareable insights, draft a LinkedIn post from the most interesting one, generate five short-form hooks from the examples in the piece, and outline a newsletter intro. Edit each for your voice and platform context. Done.

HubSpot's 2025 State of Content Marketing report found that content teams using AI for repurposing produced 3x more published content per person without increasing headcount — and saw engagement rates on repurposed content that matched original content creation. 2

### SEO and content strategy: AI as a research tool, not a content factory

The creators who've gotten AI wrong for SEO are the ones who've used it to pump out keyword-stuffed articles at volume. Google's algorithm updates have been explicitly targeting this pattern, and the results for those creators have not been good.

The creators who've gotten it right are using AI for keyword and topic research, content gap analysis, and title testing — and then writing the actual content themselves or with AI as a co-pilot rather than a ghostwriter. Ask AI what questions are underserved in your content category, what topics your audience searches for that you haven't covered, what a piece on X would need to include to rank for its primary keyword. Use AI's research capacity, apply your creative and experiential judgment.

The SEO opportunity for content creators in 2026 is also in AEO — answer engine optimization for AI search tools. When someone asks Perplexity or Claude about a topic you've written about, your content should be cited. That requires specific structural elements: a direct answer sentence early, a FAQ section, clear H2 structure. AI can help you retrofit existing content for these requirements faster than writing from scratch.

### What this means for content creators building AI workflows

The content creators building durable AI-assisted practices are doing something specific: they're using AI to expand what they can produce without diluting their voice, not to replace the original thinking that makes their content worth reading. AI handles research synthesis, repurposing mechanics, and distribution formatting. The creator handles the angle, the examples, the honesty, and the edit that makes everything sound human.

MakerSquare is a 2-week in-person AI builder program in Austin, TX — built for operators, founders, and professionals who want to build real AI tools, not just use them. Content creators and media professionals attend to build specific AI-assisted workflows — research systems, repurposing pipelines, audience tools — not just to explore what's possible. See the [curriculum](/curriculum) for specifics.

The first draft was always the easy part. AI just made it faster to get there — which means the real competitive advantage now is everything that happens after it.

Frequently asked questions

How should content creators use AI without sounding generic?

The key is using AI for structure, research, and first drafts, then rewriting with your specific voice, examples, and perspective. AI output without human editing sounds like AI — and audiences notice. The best workflow is to treat AI as a research assistant and draft engine, then spend the same time you saved doing the editing pass that makes the content sound like you.

What are the best AI tools for content creators in 2026?

Claude and ChatGPT are the most versatile for research, drafting, and editing. Descript or Adobe Podcast for audio and video editing. Midjourney or Ideogram for image generation. Opus Clip for repurposing long-form video into short clips. For SEO specifically, tools like Surfer SEO or Clearscope help optimize content against search intent. Most creators don't need all of these — pick based on where you spend the most time.

Will AI replace content creators?

AI is replacing commoditized content — templated SEO articles, generic social copy, basic product descriptions. It's not replacing creators who have a distinct point of view, a recognizable voice, and an audience that specifically wants their perspective. The creators under pressure are the ones whose value was producing volume of average content. The ones thriving are those whose value is originality, authority, and trust.

How do content creators use AI for repurposing?

The most common repurposing workflow: take a long-form piece (blog post, podcast, YouTube video transcript) and ask AI to extract a LinkedIn post, three Twitter threads, a newsletter intro, and five short-form video hooks from the same material. What used to take 3–4 hours of additional work now takes 30 minutes of AI-assisted extraction and editing. Repurposing ROI is often higher than creating new content.

# AI for E-Commerce: What's Actually Working in 2026

> AI for e-commerce in 2026: real data on what

[← Blog](/blog)

AI at Work

## AI for e-commerce: what's actually working in 2026.

Marliis Schneider

July 20, 2026

5 min read

![AI for e-commerce: what](../images/blog/ai-ecommerce-2026-og.webp)

Key takeaways

- 75% of retailers say AI agents will be essential to their business by 2026, per Salesforce's survey of 8,350 shoppers and 1,700 retail decision-makers.

- There's a real scaling gap: nearly half of $5B+ companies have scaled AI into production, compared with just 29% of companies under $100M in revenue.

- Real example: a sustainable beauty brand used AI-driven lifecycle personalization to get 40–50% more customers into long-term subscriptions.

- The winning move for smaller stores isn't chasing every AI feature — it's picking one real use case and actually shipping it, instead of piloting it forever.

For most small and mid-sized e-commerce businesses, the AI opportunity isn't a mystery — it's a gap. Big retailers are scaling AI into production; smaller stores are mostly still experimenting. The winning move for a smaller store isn't matching a multi-billion-dollar retailer's AI budget — it's picking one real use case, like personalized recommendations or AI-handled customer service, and actually shipping it instead of leaving it in pilot mode.

### AI in e-commerce is moving fast — and most stores aren't keeping up

Salesforce's sixth Connected Shoppers Report, surveying 8,350 shoppers and 1,700 retail decision-makers, found that 75% of retailers now say AI agents will be essential to their business by 2026. That's not a niche opinion anymore — it's close to consensus among people actually running retail businesses.

But adoption isn't even across company size. McKinsey's State of AI research found that nearly half of companies with more than $5 billion in revenue have scaled AI into production, compared with just 29% of companies under $100 million in revenue. Small and mid-sized e-commerce businesses are adopting AI — they're just far less likely to get past the pilot stage than a large retailer with a dedicated AI team.

### Where AI is actually paying off for online stores

The clearest wins are narrow and specific, not "AI running your store." Personalized product recommendations and lifecycle marketing — using a customer's real purchase and browsing history to decide what they see next — is one of the highest-leverage use cases available. One sustainable beauty brand, Wild, used AI-driven lifecycle personalization to get 40–50% more customers to sign up for long-term subscriptions, a concrete result tied directly to their own customer data, not a generic AI feature.

AI-handled customer service for repetitive questions — order status, return policy, sizing — is the other clear win. It doesn't replace a support team, but it removes the repetitive load from one, freeing people for the complex or emotional conversations that actually need judgment.

### Why most small e-commerce AI projects stall

The gap between big retailers and small stores isn't access to AI tools — anyone can sign up for one. It's that most small e-commerce AI projects stop at the pilot stage: a chatbot gets bolted onto the storefront, it isn't connected to real order or customer data, it gives generic answers, and it gets quietly abandoned within a few months. That pattern shows up broadly — roughly two-thirds of companies experimenting with generative AI never scale it into an ongoing part of the business.

The stores actually seeing results skipped the generic version. They connected AI directly to their real store data — order history, product catalog, customer segments — from the start, which is exactly what turns a demo into something that keeps working after the novelty wears off.

### What this means for small and mid-sized online stores

You don't need a data science team to close this gap. You need one real use case — personalization, customer service, or inventory forecasting — built around your actual store data instead of a generic tool. MakerSquare's [use cases](/use-cases) cover exactly this pattern: connecting an AI agent to real business data so it does something specific and useful, instead of being a chatbot that answers generic questions.

The online stores that pull ahead here won't be the ones that adopted the most AI tools. They'll be the ones that picked one thing worth automating and actually finished it.

Frequently asked questions

What AI tools actually work for small e-commerce businesses?

The proven use cases are personalized product recommendations and lifecycle marketing, and AI-handled customer service for common questions (order status, returns, sizing). Both connect AI directly to your store's real data — not a generic chatbot bolted on top.

How much can AI improve e-commerce conversion rates?

Results vary widely by implementation, but real examples exist: one sustainable beauty brand using AI-driven lifecycle personalization saw 40-50% more customers sign up for long-term subscriptions. The gap between a generic AI feature and one built around your actual customer data is large.

Is AI customer service good enough to replace a human for online stores?

For a narrow set of repetitive questions — order status, return policy, sizing — yes, and it frees up humans for the complex or emotional conversations that actually need judgment. It's not a full replacement for a support team, but it removes the repetitive load from one.

Do I need a developer to add AI to my online store?

No. The store owners getting real value from AI aren't the most technical people — they're the ones who understand their products and customers well enough to know what's worth automating. Modern AI tools can be directed in plain language and connected to store data without custom engineering.

What's the biggest reason AI projects fail for small e-commerce businesses?

Stopping at the pilot stage. Roughly two-thirds of companies that experiment with generative AI never scale it into a real, ongoing part of the business — often because the first attempt was a generic tool that was never connected to real store and customer data.
